newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. African academic urges pact to spur growth.
newsitem.headline: S. African academic urges pact to spur growth.

text.p: A South African academic has urged political stakeholders to enter a development pact to ensure a period of sustained higher economic growth.

Political analyst Lawrence Schlemmer said on Monday although there had been encouraging signs that the three-year-old African National Congress-led government was getting to grips with governing, there were still some worrying negative trends.

"Government delivery is improving, political stability and predictability are clearly stronger, the government seems to be taking crime control more seriously and macro-economic policy is consistent," Schlemmer said in his latest political analysis for the South African Chamber of Business.
On the negative side tension between labour, government and business continued on critical issues such as macro-economic discipline, labour market flexibility and approaches to job creation.
Government was also barely holding its own against the forces of corruption and the non-payment of rates and service charges.
In addition, its approach to education and health involved high-risk policies which could be costly.
"Perhaps one could draw these trends together by saying that government is genuinely trying to come to grips with the problem of governing a fractious society," Schlemmer said.
In the context of the "bigger picture" of emerging markets, however, South Africa looked somewhat shakier.

It was losing vital skills in the public and private sectors and social spending was rising while spending on economic services and basic infrastructure was falling to internationally embarrassing levels.

While organised labour in other countries had accepted the challenge of promoting the cost-effectiveness of labour, South African labour had "decided first to fight an economic cold war with capital and now with government itself", Schlemmer said.

Against this background, South Africa continued to merely "muddle through" and it was difficult to see how the government, with an election looming in 1999, could avoid making the kind of trade-offs that would simply entrench this trend.

The only alternative was a pact between opposing interests and stakeholders with Deputy President Thabo Mbeki using his strategic skills to unite all ministers under the Growth, Employment and Redistribution programme.
Schlemmer doubted whether such a pact would be possible, and said that it was likely that government would continue its muddling.
But he said this implied continued slow growth and it was likely that South Africa could be passed by other emerging economies competing for investment and export markets.
